source.title: The Growth Engine
source.summary: The Solow growth model, steady states, convergence failures, and why human capital is the missing variable.
source.author: Islamic Economics
source.body_text: The Solow growth model is the workhorse of growth economics. An economy produces output using capital and labor. Each year, some output is saved and invested. But capital depreciates, and diminishing returns set in. The key insight: capital accumulation alone can't sustain growth forever. Only technological progress drives long-run growth. The model predicts convergence: poor countries should grow faster. But many Muslim-majority countries haven't converged. Pakistan's per-capita growth has been anemic for decades. Indonesia did better. Malaysia succeeded. The pattern isn't about Islam. It's about institutions and governance. This episode extends the model to include human capital, where the Islamic tradition's emphasis on ilm (knowledge) should be an advantage, but modern Muslim-majority states have largely failed to translate that tradition into actual educational investment.

linkedin.post: The Solow growth model is economics' workhorse for understanding national growth. Its core insight: capital accumulation alone can't sustain long-term growth due to diminishing returns. Only technological progress drives lasting prosperity. The model makes a bold prediction: poor countries should grow faster than rich ones and eventually converge. Reality tells a different story. Pakistan's per-capita growth has been anemic for decades. Malaysia succeeded. Indonesia performed well. The pattern isn't about Islam or culture—it's about institutions, governance, and critically, human capital. The Islamic intellectual tradition has always emphasized 'ilm' (knowledge) as fundamental. This should be a natural advantage, yet many Muslim-majority countries haven't fully leveraged this in their modern development strategies. When we extend the Solow model to include human capital, the convergence story changes dramatically. Knowledge compounds without diminishing returns. Listen: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-re-2

short_video.title: Why Poor Countries Don't Catch Up
short_video.hook: The world's most famous economic model got it completely wrong
short_video.voiceover: The Solow model predicted poor countries would catch up to rich ones through capital accumulation. Build factories, grow the economy. Simple. But Pakistan's growth has been disappointing for decades while Malaysia succeeded. The missing variable? Human capital. Capital depreciates every year. Knowledge compounds forever. The Islamic tradition always emphasized ilm - knowledge - as fundamental. When economists added human capital to the Solow model, everything changed. It's not about having more machines. It's about having better minds to use them.
